Building

Verdnt Group

I co-founded Verdnt Group with Diego Sanchez Tirado. We’re building Verdnt Studio, a tool for food and drink teams developing new drinks. The goal is to help them turn market research into product ideas they can test.

Co-founder

A closer look

Verdnt Studio brings together research from social media and retail shelves to help teams decide what to make next. I work with clients to understand what they need and build the software.

Our client work includes software that combines market research with a company’s product information to suggest new products. Teams can check the sources behind each suggestion before deciding what to test.

Trus

I co-founded Trus with Diego Sanchez Tirado to help people create software for their own work. The idea was to describe what you needed and have AI build a workspace for it. Trus is now retired.

Strategy

Find the niche the incumbent ignores.

HyperPay is a payment processor in a crowded market, and the obvious pitch was a better payment product. We looked at the cash merchants leave sitting idle instead, and the working-capital advance was the idea that landed with the judges. When you can’t beat the incumbents head on, look for what they’ve stopped paying attention to.

From: HyperPay case competition, 2026

Check that the audience exists before you build.

I built Forge, an incubator for student nonprofits, before I knew anyone wanted it, and we had to cut it back. At FStea I pushed the target customer toward college students because that’s where the drink already fit. Both taught me to start where the customer already is and to pressure-test the assumption before scaling it.

From: Homer Humanities and FStea

Find the bottleneck before solving everything.

Trus started as a huge, vague problem: describe the software you need and have AI assemble it. We made progress once we picked the one constraint that mattered most, how long each generated piece took to appear, and worked on that first. I know I tend to let scope grow, so I now decide early where to go deep and where to stay narrow.

From: Trus

Commit to a decision, then say what you’d watch.

Most real decisions get made with incomplete data. Sitting on the fence doesn’t make the data better. I’d rather pick a path, say why, and name the risks and the next thing to check.

From: my interview notes, and economics

A problem gets fixable once you can measure it.

At FStea I kept a spreadsheet with a row for every campus store that sold the drink. Once the numbers sat in one place, the team could see which moves were working. I also learned to check the denominator first. A unit price per case and a unit price per bottle look the same until they don’t.

From: FStea, 2025, and Verdnt client work

Tech & AI

On my own time, I run a small team of AI agents that handle my coding and notes.

Let the model interpret. Let code handle anything that has to be right.

In a quoting product, a wrong answer costs real money. A language model is good at reading a messy part description, so it gets that job. The pricing math stays in plain code. Then I add a guardrail and a way to know whether it worked.

From: Camber, 2026

Confidence isn’t correctness.

A model can be sure and wrong at the same time, so I never let its confidence alone decide whether something ships. My Camber demo answers a deliberately vague request with “REVIEW REQUIRED” instead of a guess. Software that says when it’s unsure is easier to trust.

From: the Camber homepage demo

A tool only helps if people trust it.

At Morgan Stanley, the agents I built only mattered once analysts understood them, so explaining them to non-technical colleagues mattered as much as the code. At Verdnt, every suggestion shows its sources. Nobody should have to take a recommendation on faith, including ours.

From: Morgan Stanley and Verdnt Group

Check what should have been there and wasn’t.

When I built my own job-search pipeline, almost every bug was a silent drop: real postings lost to a broken source or an overeager filter. Looking at what came through wasn’t enough. Now I also look for what’s missing.

From: a personal automation project, 2026

AI is a tool, and people stay responsible for it.

I’d rather build AI that helps people do more than AI that replaces them. In the winning Stanford policy memo I co-wrote, our part proposed short in-person checks so students can explain their reasoning out loud.

From: philosophy coursework and the Stanford memo, 2026

Values

Consistent, unglamorous work compounds.

Volunteering with the Ethical Culture Society, I wrote cards, made sandwiches and helped with donation drives. It taught me I do my best work as a reliable teammate, not only when I’m the one in charge.

From: volunteering in Silicon Valley

Finish what you start.

The values I hold at work are respect for my own work, respect for the people involved, and taking ideas and commitments all the way through. When something goes wrong, I tell the right person early and say what I plan to do.

From: my interview notes

No fate, only action and reaction.

That’s the rule in Statesman, the board game I designed, and roughly how I think about life too. In my philosophy essays I keep landing in the same place: a choice can be voluntary without being free of past experience. Schopenhauer said it best: “Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.”

From: Statesman and my essays on free will

Watch the tape.

Coaching karate, I filmed my students’ sparring rounds and went through them technique by technique, looking for the one thing to fix. I still work at that level of detail, whether the tape is a sparring round or a spreadsheet.

From: coaching at Okaigan Karate

What I put first.

When I wrote down what I value most, I named three things: the people close to me, my health, and the work.

From: a note to myself, 2026

Books

The unread books on my shelf are a reminder of what I don’t know and might yet discover. These are the ones I’ve read and keep thinking about, with what each one left me.

My Brilliant Friend

A friendship is a choice two people make again and again, with no legal or family tie holding it in place. Ferrante makes the things left unsaid between Elena and Lila as loud as the things they say.

Elena Ferrante · my favorite novel

Diagnostic Political Philosophy

It asks how to decide well without the full picture, which is what governing in an age of misinformation requires. That question followed me into economics, where most real decisions get made with incomplete data.

Hans Sluga · I helped research and edit it

Beyond Good and Evil

I read it across a desk from Professor Sluga in our weekly meetings. What stuck wasn’t any one answer. It was the expectation that the next question is always coming, and that I’d better have read chapter twelve.

Friedrich Nietzsche · read with Hans Sluga

The Order of Things

I helped build more than 200 pages of material for Sluga’s graduate seminar on it. Writing for graduate students taught me to break a hard idea into steps someone else can follow.

Michel Foucault · seminar material

Three books on meritocracy

I read them side by side for a Stanford writing class. Merit turned out to be a moving target. Institutions keep redefining it, and the definition decides who wins. Kirn adds the difference between performing competence and having it. The question I’m left with is what merit should be.

Sandel, The Tyranny of Merit · Markovits, The Meritocracy Trap · Kirn, Lost in the Meritocracy

Republic and Apology

The cave, and the case for the examined life. Plato’s city run by philosopher-kings became the premise of Statesman, the board game I designed.

Plato · UChicago summer program, 2022
